title: werden and wollen
summary: Talking about intentions, plans, and simple future-oriented meaning.
whyItMatters: 'Wollen' states a clear intention, while 'werden' describes becoming or, with an infinitive, explicitly marks a future event. Both verbs help distinguish a desired action from a predicted or developing situation.

mentalModel.title: Wollen points to intention
mentalModel.content: Use 'wollen' when the subject actively intends or wants to do something: 'Ich will den Termin ändern.'

mentalModel.title: Werden points to change or future
mentalModel.content: Use 'werden' alone with a noun or adjective for becoming, and with a final infinitive to mark future meaning.

mentalModel.title: Both verbs create a sentence frame
mentalModel.content: When another verb is present, the conjugated verb stands in position two and the infinitive closes the sentence.

ruleBlocks.title: Use wollen for a firm intention
ruleBlocks.content: Conjugate 'wollen' and place the intended action as an infinitive at the end: 'Wir wollen morgen anrufen.'

ruleBlocks.title: Use werden for becoming
ruleBlocks.content: Combine 'werden' with a noun or adjective: 'Sie wird Ärztin' or 'Der Termin wird später.'

ruleBlocks.title: Use werden plus infinitive for explicit future
ruleBlocks.content: Place the infinitive at the end: 'Ich werde den Termin morgen bestätigen.'

ruleBlocks.title: Prefer present tense when time is already clear
ruleBlocks.content: German often says 'Morgen rufe ich an'; future 'werden' adds emphasis, prediction, or explicit future framing.

sentenceStructure: Only the conjugated verb carries person and number.
With another verb, the infinitive closes the sentence.
Yes-no questions begin with the conjugated form.
A future time expression often makes the simple present sufficient.

concepts: recognize explicit future with werden plus infinitive
use modal and future forms in longer sentences
use werden for passive and nuanced prediction
choose future forms according to discourse purpose

comparisons.summary: The theme lesson provides plans and schedule changes that require intention and future language.
Appointment exchanges contrast what someone wants to do with what will happen next.

examples.en: I want to arrange an appointment.
The appointment is becoming later / is being moved later.

examples.de: Wann willst du den Arzt anrufen?
examples.en: When do you want to call the doctor?

examples.de: Am Freitag treffe ich meine Kollegin.
examples.en: I am meeting my colleague on Friday.

commonMistakes.reason: The second verb remains an infinitive at the end.

commonMistakes.wrong: Use werden for every future event.
commonMistakes.correct: Use present tense when a future time expression already makes the timing clear.
commonMistakes.reason: Simple present is the normal choice for many scheduled plans.

specialCases: 'Ich will ...' can sound firm; 'ich möchte ...' is often more polite for requests.
'Werden' has several later uses, including passive voice.
Profession nouns after 'werden' normally appear without an article: 'Sie wird Ärztin.'
tips: Underline the conjugated verb and circle the final infinitive.
Transform one plan through present, wollen, and werden.
